newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Aussie dlr bandwagon stalled at chart barrier.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Aussie dlr bandwagon stalled at chart barrier.

text.p: The Australian dollar subsided to a steady finish Monday in what was rapidly becoming a well worn pattern of fruitless rallies and frustrated profit-taking.

The positive potential of last week's Federal budget had already been taken on board and the flow of samurai-related demand, while steady, was not proving as substantial as rumour suggested, leading to some modest selling.

The repeated failure to carry the struggle past US$0.7935 resistance left the currency vulnerable to sell off back to US$0.7850 or so, although dealers expected heavy new buying to emerge of the pivotal US$0.7810 chart level was approached.
By 4.45 pm (0630 GMT) the local currency was idling at US$0.7910/15 after reversing from an early US$0.7928 high but remained in line with Friday's late US$0.7907/12.

A break higher, would see trendline resistance around US$0.7960/70 tested with a good chance of revisiting July's high at 80 cents this week. Beyond that was the ultimate bull target of US$0.8050, a 5-1/2 year peak reached in May.

On the crosses, the local dollar was hovering at 85.46/56 yen from 85.62/72 late Friday and 1.1699/1710 marks from 1.1783/95 having tracked a retreating U.S. dollar lower. That saw it soften in trade weighted terms to 57.9 from 58.0.

Dealers said the continuing flow of dual currency samurai demand was encouraging for dollar bulls -- with Sweden launching 25 billion yen of bonds today -- although a much-anticipated issue from IBM had yet to make an appearance.

There were some concerns the recent sharp fall in Australian bond yields -- the 10-yr future has shot to 92.00 today from 91.00 two months ago -- would divert offshore demand, particularly to the higher-yielding New Zealand market.
However, many thought the Kiwi market too illiquid to accomodate the huge Japanese appetite for A$-denominated bonds seen throughout this year.

Another past competitor for Japanese investor interest was Canadian dollar assets, but yields there had fallen even more sharply than in Australia as the Bank of Canada followed an aggressive easing policy.

Some had seen the South African rand as a potential high yielding challenger, but it had plunged around 25 percent in value this year tarnishing it, and many other exotic high yielders, as an unacceptable currency risk.
And recent firm data here, as well as the U.S., had reduced the immediate risk of another cut in domestic rates, all of which suggested the A$ would remain attractive for a while yet.
June quarter inventories data out today were rendered largely irrelevant by the early release of Q2 GDP figures with the Federal Budget last week.

The same was true of June quarter balance of payments Tuesday which would normally be watched for the contribution of net exports to GDP. That had already been revealed at a 0.9 point detraction with exports falling and imports rising.

Of more interest will be the July current account deficit on Thursday, which is expected to be close to June's benign A$1.29 billion level thanks to an already reported three percent fall in imports. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
